# Malaria carried by mosquitoes (drainage, nets) (`malaria_mosquito`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by microscope, contagion_theory, quinine
- Core idea: The recurring fevers of marshy country are caused by a parasite in the blood that usually reaches people through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito. They breed in still, fairly clean water (pools, ditches, hoof prints, rice fields) and bite from dusk to dawn. Drain or fill standing water within a kilometre or so of houses, stock ponds with small fish that eat the larvae, pour a film of oil on puddles, sleep under a fine net tucked in on all sides, and build on dry high ground away from marsh. Yellow fever is carried the same way by a different mosquito that breeds in water jars and barrels around houses.
- Pitfalls:
  - Keeping the bad-air theory: closing windows at night helps only if it keeps mosquitoes out
  - Thinking malaria passes directly from person to person, or from drinking marsh water
  - Draining the big swamp and ignoring puddles, ditches and borrow pits near the houses
  - A net with holes or one that is not tucked in
  - Expecting one fever to give lasting immunity; malaria relapses and can be caught again
- History: egypt: 5th c. BC – Herodotus reports people in the Egyptian marshes sleeping under their fishing nets against gnats; rome: 1st c. BC–1st c. AD – Varro and Columella advise against building near marshes; india: 1897 – Ronald Ross at Secunderabad finds the parasite in an Anopheles mosquito; 1898 works out the full cycle in birds at Calcutta; africa: 1880 – Laveran sees the parasite in blood at Constantine, Algeria; europe: 1717 – Lancisi suspects marsh insects; 1898 Grassi and colleagues in Rome demonstrate transmission of human malaria by Anopheles; americas: 1881 – Finlay in Havana proposes mosquito transmission of yellow fever; 1900 Reed's commission proves it; 1904–1914 Gorgas clears the Panama Canal zone
- Read:
  - Ronald Ross, On some peculiar pigmented cells found in two mosquitos fed on malarial blood, British Medical Journal (1897)
  - Randall M. Packard, The Making of a Tropical Disease: A Short History of Malaria (2007)
  - Sonia Shah, The Fever: How Malaria Has Ruled Humankind for 500,000 Years (2010)
